---
title: "2 The score spine"
---

Session 2 builds the model every other part of the platform consumes: a weight-of-evidence
scorecard that turns an applicant's financials and bureau history into a score, a
probability of default and a band. It is gated — AUC at least {{< var score.gate >}} on
held-out applicants — and the gate cannot be negotiated. Then the session asks the question
a validator asks: held on *which* population?

## The videos

Six chapters, one idea each, in session order.

{{< yt S2-c1 >}}

Why a scorecard, when gradient boosting is available: every point of the score can be traced
to one bin of one variable, so a validator can replicate it by hand.

{{< yt S2-c2 >}}

Binning one variable by hand, then letting the optimiser do it, and reading weight of
evidence and information value off the result.

{{< yt S2-c3 >}}

From one variable to {{< var score.n_features >}}: which features carry signal and which
only look as if they do.

{{< yt S2-c4 >}}

The gate, live: drop the bureau columns and the refit fails at
{{< var score.stress.no_bureau.auc >}}. The failure is documented, not tuned away.

{{< yt S2-c5 >}}

The committed scorecard scores {{< var score.pop.everyone.auc >}} on all held-out
applicants and {{< var score.pop.booked.auc >}} on the ones the bank actually books. An AUC
without its population is incomplete.

{{< yt S2-c6 >}}

Reason codes: why each applicant got the score they got, exactly, from the model's own
arithmetic.

## Check

```bash
python verify.py
```

The scorecard line recomputes the held-out AUC from the saved model and compares it with
the gate. It passes on the committed scorecard.

## Homework with an agent

Three exercises: refit without the bureau columns and document the gate failure; catch an
agent quoting an AUC without its population; and ask an agent why the feature with the
largest coefficient explains almost none of the score. They arrive before Session 4, each
with a self-check.
